title: Agentic Architecture
goal: Given a production scenario, decide the architecture that actually fits: a stop_reason-driven loop, a hub-and-spoke coordinator, a prompt or a programmatic gate, and the right resume, fork or fresh-start call.

steps.title: An agent is a while loop, not a program
steps.inshort: An agentic loop calls the model, runs whatever tools it asked for, appends the results, and calls the model again — repeating until the model stops asking for tools.
steps.lead: Start with the piece that everything else in this domain hangs off. Your code sends a request, Claude replies, and if the reply asks for a tool you run it and send the result back. That cycle is the agent. Everything the exam asks about stopping, gating, delegating or recovering is a decision made somewhere on this cycle.
points: The Messages API is stateless: every call must resend the whole conversation, because the endpoint remembers nothing between requests.
A response is a list of content blocks plus a `stop_reason` field — not a single string of text.
A tool call arrives as a `tool_use` block; you answer it with a `tool_result` block inside a new user-role message.
Each `tool_result` must carry the `tool_use_id` from the matching `tool_use` request, or the model cannot pair them up.
steps.code:
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(model=M, messages=messages, tools=tools)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
steps.why: The loop has no built-in sense of completion. The model cannot end your program for you — it can only say what it wants next, and the API gives you one structured field that says whether it wants a tool or is finished. Control lives in your code, driven by that field.
steps.contrast: People reach for natural language: check whether the reply text contains done, or set a fixed iteration cap and call it completion detection. Both look like they work in a demo, because a demo has one happy path. In production the model writes text and calls a tool in the same response, so any check on the text fires early.
steps.exam: This is the foundation task, and most Domain 1 questions reduce to it. If you can state that `stop_reason` is the only authoritative loop-control signal, you can answer the stopping questions without knowing the scenario.
steps.takeaway: The model asks, your code decides. `stop_reason` is the switch.

steps.title: One field decides whether the loop continues
steps.inshort: `stop_reason == "tool_use"` means keep looping. `stop_reason == "end_turn"` means stop. Nothing else decides.
steps.lead: Two values do all the work, and the exam tests the pair constantly. Read the field, not the prose.
points: `tool_use` — the model wants a tool run. Execute it and loop again.
`end_turn` — the model is finished. Exit the loop and return the answer.
`max_tokens` and `stop_sequence` are also stopping states you must handle, because the task may not be done.
`refusal` means the model declined, which is not the same as finishing successfully.
steps.caption: The cycle your code owns. The back edge exists only while stop_reason says tool_use.
steps.why: Because it is a structured field produced by the API rather than text produced by the model, it cannot be reworded, reformatted, or buried in a long explanation. It is the one signal your code can branch on without guessing.
steps.contrast: Parsing the assistant text is the temptation — it avoids one API call and looks cheap. But a single response can carry both a text block and a `tool_use` block, so a text-based check exits while tools are still pending. That is the classic premature-termination bug.
steps.exam: The exam's preferred answer is `stop_reason`-driven control, and it usually appears next to a distractor that sounds more efficient. The other stopping states are tested as a secondary detail.
steps.takeaway: Branch on the field. If it is not `tool_use`, your loop is finished looping.

steps.title: Anti-pattern one: parsing natural language for completion
steps.inshort: Checking if the reply contains words like "done" or "finished" to decide whether to stop the loop.
steps.lead: It feels intuitive and works in early testing. It is also the most brittle choice you can make.
points: Natural language is ambiguous — the model might narrate reasoning ("let me check that") without calling a tool, or call a tool with no narration.
Phrasing drifts across prompts and model versions — a string match that works today silently breaks tomorrow.
The structured contract does not drift: a turn that wants a tool returns `stop_reason: tool_use`, full stop.

ask.q: A support agent loops over `client.messages.create` with tools. A teammate proposes exiting the loop whenever the assistant text contains the words done or resolved, to save an API call. Production shows the agent sometimes stops mid-task with a partial answer. What is the bug?
options: A) The model sometimes narrates reasoning without emitting a tool call, so the text check fires early
B) The model stops emitting the word done after a prompt tweak, so the loop runs forever
D) The API ignores the text and only respects stop_reason

steps.why: Prose parsing fails both ways: it stops early when the model narrates, and runs forever when the model's wording changes.
steps.contrast: A string match looks deterministic in a test case. In production the model's wording is not a contract.
steps.exam: The exam will phrase this as a production symptom — partial answers, infinite loops — and ask which change you would ship. The fix is always: branch on stop_reason.
steps.takeaway: Text is for humans. stop_reason is for code.

steps.title: Anti-pattern two: iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism
steps.inshort: Running a fixed number of iterations and returning whatever you have, instead of checking stop_reason.
steps.lead: Capping iterations is a legitimate safety guard. The anti-pattern is using that cap as the primary way to decide the work is done.
points: If your loop's real stopping logic is "run exactly five iterations," you cut off useful work when the task needed six, and waste turns when it finished in two.
The cap is blind to whether the model is actually finished.
The correct design branches on `stop_reason` to decide completion, and keeps a generous iteration cap only as a backstop against runaways.
Caps guard; they do not decide.
steps.code:
# guard, not decision
MAX_ITER = 50  # generous backstop
while iter < MAX_ITER:
    resp = client.messages.create(...)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    # ... run tools, append results
    iter += 1
# iter == MAX_ITER means something went wrong — alert, don't silently return
steps.why: A cap that is also the completion logic produces two failure modes: truncation (task needed more turns) and waste (task finished early). Both are invisible until you check results.
steps.contrast: Setting MAX_ITER=5 looks safe in a demo where tasks finish in 3. In production the distribution shifts.
steps.exam: Expect a scenario where an agent "sometimes returns incomplete answers." The trap answer is "increase the cap." The fix is: branch on stop_reason, keep a generous cap as a guardrail.
steps.takeaway: Caps are guardrails. stop_reason is the decision.

steps.title: Anti-pattern three: checking for assistant text as a completion signal
steps.inshort: If the assistant returned a text block, conclude the agent is finished.
steps.lead: This breaks because the model frequently emits a text block alongside a `tool_use` block, narrating what it is about to do while also requesting the tool.
points: Seeing text present, your loop concludes the agent is done, returns the half-formed narration, and never runs the tool.
This is the bug at the heart of premature loop termination: checking `response.content[0].type == "text"` ends the loop early.
The presence of text tells you nothing definitive about completion. Only `stop_reason` does.
steps.why: A single response can contain both text narration and tool_use blocks. The text narrates intent; stop_reason declares completion.
steps.contrast: The content array describes what the model produced. stop_reason describes what the model intends next.
steps.exam: The exam shows a loop that checks for text blocks and asks why it fails on multi-step tasks. The answer: text and tool_use can appear together.

steps.title: Three wrong signals versus the one right signal
steps.inshort: Every anti-pattern routes the decision through a proxy; only stop_reason is authoritative.
steps.lead: The sound loop is a while driven by stop_reason: continue while tool_use, stop on end_turn, explicitly handle max_tokens and refusal. A safety cap is a guardrail, never the primary logic.
points: Natural-language parsing trusts wording
Iteration caps trust a counter
Content-type checks trust block shape
None of those proxies is the model's actual statement of intent
steps.why: The unifying fix for all three anti-patterns is single: read stop_reason and branch on it.
steps.contrast: New variations appear constantly ("stop when response < 50 tokens", "stop after particular tool"). All fail the same way: they trust a proxy. If you can ask "Is this decision made by stop_reason or a proxy for it?" you can classify any loop on sight.
steps.exam: When the exam shows four loop designs, the right one branches on stop_reason and treats caps as backstops. The three wrong ones each lean on an anti-pattern.
steps.takeaway: Structured signal over prose, one authoritative field over three proxies.

steps.title: Check your understanding
steps.inshort: An agent occasionally returns an empty or half-written answer. Its loop ends as soon as the assistant response includes any text content block.
steps.lead: Identify the anti-pattern and the fix.

ask.q: An agent occasionally returns an empty or half-written answer. Its loop ends as soon as the assistant response includes any text content block. What is the best fix?
options: A) Stop using text-block presence as the completion signal and branch the loop on `stop_reason` instead
B) Add a longer system-prompt instruction telling Claude to always finish before replying
C) Lower `max_tokens` so the model produces shorter, more decisive responses
D) Retry the request automatically whenever the answer looks short

steps.why: The bug is anti-pattern three: checking for text presence instead of stop_reason. The model emits text alongside tool_use. Only A addresses the root cause.
steps.contrast: B relies on prompting (probabilistic). C truncates answers (counterproductive). D papers over the bug without fixing the logic.
steps.exam: This exact question structure appears: a production symptom, four fixes, one structural and three superficial.
steps.takeaway: The fix is always: read stop_reason.

steps.title: Exam lens — the one question that decides every Domain 1 loop answer
steps.inshort: Ask: "Does this make the loop more dependent on stop_reason or less?"
steps.lead: Answers that add prose parsing, lean harder on a counter, or inspect content shape all move away from the authoritative signal and are wrong by construction. The single answer that moves toward branching on stop_reason, even if phrased plainly, is the one to choose.
points: Prose parsing → less dependent on stop_reason → wrong
Iteration cap as primary logic → less dependent on stop_reason → wrong
Content-type check → less dependent on stop_reason → wrong
Branch on stop_reason, cap as guardrail → more dependent on stop_reason → correct
steps.why: This lens collapses a four-option question into a one-question test. It is the same lens you should apply when reviewing real agent code.
steps.contrast: Most wrong answers in Domain 1 add a moving part: another agent, another cap, another prompt clause. The pattern is to prefer the signal that already exists and the guarantee that cannot be argued with.
steps.exam: Expect the scenario to describe a production symptom and ask which change you would ship. Sort the options by whether they add a probability or a guarantee.
steps.takeaway: Stop_reason is the source of truth. Every other signal is a proxy.
